title: CAMPER: mechanistic artificial intelligence for designing peptides that target MRSA persisters

paper_content.abstract: Developing short, stable, and potent antimicrobial peptides is a promising strategy to combat antibiotic resistance and persistence. We present CAMPER (Constraint-driven AMP Engineering with Ranking), a mechanistic artificial intelligence framework that integrates machine learning with biophysical ranking to prioritize membrane-targeting peptides effective against persister and biofilm forms of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. We apply CAMPER to identify WP-CAMPER1 (12mer) that kills S. aureus MW2 at an minimal inhibitory concentration of 4 µg/mL. A 2% topical WP-CAMPER1 formulation reduces S. aureus MW2 burden by 2.5 log (p < 0.0002) in a murine prophylactic skin infection model, while its D-enantiomer, WP-CAMPER1-d, achieves 1.37 log (p < 0.0001) reduction in an established biofilm infection model. Single-cell analysis using a high-throughput microfluidic system shows that WP-CAMPER1-d reduces exponential-phase persisters of S. aureus USA300, and, in a deep-seated murine thigh infection model, decreases stationary-phase S. aureus MW2 persisters by 1.6 log (p < 0.0001).
paper_content.introduction:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identifies antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as an urgent global public health threat.1,2 Annually, over 2.8 million antimicrobial-resistant infections occur in the United States, resulting in more than 35,000 deaths1, with Staphylococcus aureus being a leading cause of severe healthcare-associated infections, including sepsis, pneumonia, endocarditis, and osteomyelitis.3 The CDC estimates that methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) alone accounts for over 70,000 serious infections and nearly 9,000 deaths each year,4 while vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA), even though it remains rare, is another emerging threat.5 Further compounding the AMR challenge, S. aureus can transition into low-energy states, such as persisters,6 and form biofilms,7 adaptations that enable it to evade conventional antibiotic therapy and contribute to chronic and relapsing infections,8 underscoring the urgent need for alternative therapies.

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent a promising class of therapeutic agents capable of targeting drug-resistant bacteria and physiologically distinct forms such as persisters and biofilms, without promoting resistance.8,9 Unlike conventional antibiotics, which primarily target active biosynthetic pathways in metabolically active bacterial cells,10 AMPs primarily disrupt the bacterial membranes,11 an appealing strategy against both persisters and biofilms, as membrane disruption occurs independently of the bacterial growth state.12 Precisely designing AMPs for selective bacterial membrane disruption using traditional methods13,14 relies on rational modifications to properties such as charge, hydrophobicity, helicity, and amphipathicity.11 These approaches are often constrained by the time and resources required to explore complex sequence spaces. As an alternative, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful tool for AMP discovery, enabling rapid candidate prediction by identifying patterns in sequence and physicochemical data.15-28

ML-based approaches provide important statistical associations but overlook key mechanistic features, such as membrane selectivity and structural feasibility, limiting their biological relevance.15-28 Several prior studies have incorporated physicochemical and structural features into ML classifiers, including hydrophobicity, net charge, and helix-forming propensity, as part of their feature sets.17,18,29 While these approaches capture statistical associations between biophysical properties and activity, they treat these properties as input variables for supervised learning rather than as explicit mechanistic constraints. As a result, they overlook the biophysical requirements that define membrane-active AMP behavior, such as selective membrane interaction, amphipathic folding, and the structural feasibility of helical conformations.

To address this gap, we developed a Mechanistic Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework that integrates an ML model with a biophysically informed scoring function. We refer to our hybrid model as CAMPER (Constraint-driven AMP Engineering with Ranking), reflecting its dual-stage approach: an ML classifier trained on experimental AMP data, and a biophysical scoring function that imposes mechanistic constraints. The ML component scores peptides based on key physicochemical properties required for membrane activity,11 effectively ranking candidates by both statistical likelihood and mechanistic plausibility. Our ML classifier, a random forest trained on chemical, structural, and sequence features, provides high-throughput probabilistic predictions of antimicrobial activity. The biophysical scoring function evaluates the potential of each peptide to function as a membrane-active AMP based on well-established biophysical properties: net charge, hydrophobicity, hydrophobic moment, and helicity.8,11,24

We developed CAMPER to prioritize membrane-active AMPs with the specific aim of targeting drug-tolerant bacterial phenotypes such as biofilms and persister cells. We applied CAMPER to screen a mastoparan-derived peptide library and identified WP-CAMPER1 as the top candidate. In a proof of concept study, we evaluated WP-CAMPER1 across a series of in vitro and in vivo models, confirming its potent activity against the staphylococcal membrane, a property that strongly predicts efficacy against persisters.8,30 Then, we confirmed its activity against drug-resistant S. aureus, including biofilms and persister populations. We developed the D-enantiomer of WP-CAMPER1, and tested it in the Mother Machine,31,32 a single-cell microfluidic assay used to evaluate activity against rare exponential-phase persisters, and confirmed its efficacy against rare exponential phase persisters. The Mother Machine enables real-time tracking of individual bacteria under controlled conditions that simulate in vivo environments, including nutrient limitation and dynamic drug exposure.31 Finally, we confirmed the anti-persister potency of WP-CAMPER1-d against stationary phase persisters in a well-established neutropenic murine deep-tissue thigh infection model, which is widely used to assess anti-persister therapeutics with translational relevance for systemic clinical applications.12,30,33
paper_content.results:
To advance the discovery of target-specific AMPs, we focused on membrane-active peptides against S. aureus and developed CAMPERT as a dual-component in silico pipeline that combines a machine learning classifier trained on curated AMP sequences with a scoring function based on four biophysical constraints relevant to the membrane-disruptive activity of α-helical peptides: net charge, hydrophobicity, hydrophobic moment, and helicity (Figure 1). We focused on α-helical peptides because they are structurally simple, synthetically accessible, and tunable, making them ideal candidates for rational design and optimization using computational pipelines like CAMPER.

Dataset Assembly and Feature Engineering
We began by training a random forest (RF) classifier to serve as the first component of the CAMPER pipeline, predicting the antimicrobial activity of peptides against S. aureus. To construct the ML model, we collected 3,961 peptide sequences with MIC measurements against S. aureus from the Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP). The database included 2,280 sequences we labeled as active (MIC ≤ 32 µg/mL) and 1,431 as inactive (MIC ≥ 64 µg/mL), excluding those with MIC values between these thresholds. After removing sequences containing non-standard amino acids, we retained a final dataset of 3,660 unique peptide sequences.

To assess model performance on unseen data, we first created a stratified 80 to 20 random split of the dataset. The 20% portion served as a holdout set. The training set contained 2,928 peptides, with 1,674 active peptides (57.2%) and 1,254 inactive peptides (42.8%). The holdout set contained 732 peptides, with 419 active peptides (57.2%) and 313 inactive peptides (42.8%). These proportions match the class distribution of the full dataset, which consisted of 2,093 active peptides (57.2%) and 1,567 inactive peptides (42.8%). Next, we generated a total of 66 physicochemical descriptors to characterize each peptide and train the model on properties that may influence antimicrobial activity (Table S1). Additionally, we computed the Morgan fingerprint (2048-bit, radius 4) to represent the substructural features of each peptide, resulting in a combined feature set of 2,114 descriptors.

Model Training, Evaluation, and Robustness
We assessed performance using the homology aware 5-fold cross-validation procedure described in the Methods. Based on the sensitivity analysis, we selected an 80% similarity threshold as the most stable and well-balanced cutoff for homology-aware evaluation (Figure S1). We evaluated several combinations of feature representations and classifiers; specifically, sequence-derived n-grams, and ProtBERT embeddings paired with random forest, XGBoost, and logistic regression. Across these combinations, models built on physicochemical descriptors consistently outperformed those trained on sequence-derived n-grams and ProtBERT embeddings, and random forests produced the strongest overall discrimination (Figure 2A-B, Table S2). The corresponding confusion matrices for all feature–model combinations are shown in Figure S2, which illustrates the distribution of correct and incorrect predictions under homology-aware cross-validation.

The RF model achieved an accuracy of 78% on the holdout set, with a precision of 79%, recall of 83%, F1 score of 81%, and AUC of 82%. Under the homology-aware 5-fold cross-validation scheme, the RF classifier showed lower overall discrimination than in the random split, with a mean cross-validated AUC of 70% (Figure 2C). This decrease reflects the stricter evaluation created by grouping peptides with substantial sequence similarity into the same fold, which reduces the amount of overlapping sequence information across training and validation subsets. The confusion matrix shows the distribution of true positive, false positive, true negative, and false negative predictions in the holdout set (Figure 2E). As shown in the calibration plot in Figure S3, the RF classifier produces reasonably calibrated probability estimates, with a Brier score of 0.156 indicating good overall alignment between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies.

To validate model reliability, we performed y-randomization, shuffling the activity labels in the training data while preserving the feature values. After 100 iterations, the randomized models achieved an average accuracy of 52%, significantly lower than the 80% accuracy of the original model, confirming that the observed performance is not due to random associations within the data.

We evaluated feature importance within the random forest classifier by ranking features according to their mean impurity-based importance scores (Figure 2F). GRAVY ranked highest, followed by MolLogP and BertzCT. Several BCUT2D descriptors, along with molar refractivity and the Kappa shape indices, also appeared among the top contributors. Hydrophobic moment was likewise ranked highly. Overall, the model relied most on descriptors related to hydrophobicity, charge distribution, polarizability, and amphipathic structure.

Biophysical Scorer Integration
To refine the selection of peptides predicted by the first component of CAMPER, we integrated a biophysical scoring function alongside the RF classifier to generate the final ranking. The biophysical scoring function was designed to prioritize α-helical, membrane-active peptides targeting S. aureus by ranking candidates based on four key physicochemical properties: net charge, hydrophobicity, hydrophobic moment, and helicity. Detailed rationale for property selection and the mathematical transformations applied are described in the Methods section, with hyperparameter and weights of the biophysical scorer provided in Supplementary Results.

We calculated performance metrics on the held-out test set. As noted above, peptides with MIC ≤ 32 µg/mL were labeled as active, and those with MIC ≥ 64 µg/mL as inactive, with peptides in the intermediate range excluded from evaluation. Compared to the standalone RF model, which achieved a precision of 81%, CAMPER (RF combined with Biophysical Scorer) improved precision to 86%, representing a 5 percentage point increase in correctly identifying true positives among predicted actives (Table S2). Notably, the number of false positives (defined as peptides predicted as active by the model but labeled as inactive based on their MIC) decreased substantially from 92 in the RF model to just 21 with CAMPER, representing a 77% reduction (Figure 2E). This reduction aligns with the intended use of CAMPER as a prioritization framework that screens large, custom peptide libraries and aims to minimize synthesis and testing of non-active peptides. CAMPER shows lower recall and a lower AUC compared to the standalone RF model (Figure 2C, Table S2), but this decrease in recall and AUC primarily reflects the prioritization introduced by the biophysical scoring function which favors peptides consistent with an α-helical, membrane-disruptive mechanism rather than optimizing discrimination across all antimicrobial mechanisms. Analysis of peptides in the external evaluation set that were experimentally labeled as active in the dataset, predicted as active by the RF model, but deprioritized by CAMPER showed that 70% (140/200) were not predominantly α-helical based on AlphaFold2 structure predictions. These peptides and their predicted secondary structure classes are provided in Supplementary Data 1.

To assess the biophysical characteristics of peptides prioritized by CAMPER, we selected the top 50 test set predictions ranked by (i) the RF classifier alone, (ii) the biophysical scoring function alone, and (iii) the combined CAMPER score. Compared to RF-only predictions, CAMPER-ranked peptides showed higher median helicity and hydrophobic moment with tighter distributions around values characteristic of α-helical, membrane-active peptides targeting Gram-positive bacteria (Figure S4). Additionally, the integration of the biophysical scoring function within CAMPER led to improvements in prediction precision within specific regions of the biophysical feature space. For example, among peptides with hydropathy (GRAVY) between -1.19–0.26, the precision increased from 72% (RF-only) to 95% with the CAMPER dual-component model (Figure 2G), and for the 0.20–0.40 helicity range precision increased from 75% to 97% (Figure 2H). Similar improvements in precision were observed in additional regions of the biophysical feature space. Precision gains were also observed across various grand average of charge and hydrophobic moment bins (Figure 2G-I). At the same time, we observed a clear drop in precision in the highest charge interval, which includes only a small number of peptides and represents an extreme physicochemical regime that is not characteristic of most membrane-acting sequences (Figure 2I). This pattern highlights that CAMPER performs best in well-represented and biologically relevant regions of the feature space while showing reduced precision in sparse, extreme outlier bins.

Application of CAMPER to a Rationally Designed Peptide Library
To demonstrate the ability of CAMPER to prioritize potent and membrane-active AMPs, we applied the pipeline to a candidate pool derived from a natural 14-mer peptide template, using it as a proof of concept for targeted in silico screening. Details on the peptide library generation are provided in the Methods section. We screened the peptide library with CAMPER and prioritized the five top-ranked candidates for synthesis to enable rapid and efficient experimental assessment. WP-CAMPER1, the top-ranked candidate, exhibited a favorable physicochemical profile for membrane-targeting activity against Gram-positive bacteria with a GRAVY of 1.21, a hydrophobic moment of 0.538, net charge of 2.55 and a helical propensity of 83.33%. The physicochemical profiles of all five synthesized candidates are summarized in Table 1.

In vitro antimicrobial potency of the top-ranked peptides.
We evaluated the antimicrobial activity of WP-CAMPER1 followed by the next four top-ranked AMPs (WP-CAMPER2 to WP-CAMPER5), selected from the rationally designed peptide library described in the preceding section, using MIC assays against S. aureus strain MW2 (Table 1). WP-CAMPER1 exhibited a potent MIC of 4 µg/mL against S. aureus MW2. We also explored the antimicrobial robustness of the WP-CAMPER1 peptide by evaluating its antimicrobial activity under physiological salt conditions, varying pH levels, and in the presence of serum. The MIC of WP-CAMPER1 remained unchanged in the presence of monovalent and divalent salt (150 mM NaCl, 150 mM MgSO4) and at pH levels of 7.4 and 8.0, except at pH 6.8, where it increased twofold. Similarly, the MIC increased only twofold in the presence of 5% human serum (Table S3).

Validation of WP-CAMPEAR1 by traditional quantitative-structure activity relationship (QSAR)-based peptide design
We conducted a QSAR analysis of WP-CAMPER1 to evaluate the hypothesis that CAMPER effectively ranks peptide sequences for membrane-disruptive antimicrobial activity by optimizing charge, hydrophobicity, and amphipathicity. In this series of analyses, we introduced substitutions of both hydrophilic and hydrophobic amino acids on different faces of WP-CAMPER1 (Figure S5). We explored three conditions: increasing the charge, enhancing hydrophobicity, and altering both as detailed in the Methods.

The variants displayed MICs ranging from 4 to 8 µg/mL, depending on modifications to charge and hydrophobicity (Table S4). When only the charge or hydrophobicity was increased in WP-CAMPER1 (variants WP-CAMPER1-6K and WP-CAMPER1-5L8L), the antimicrobial potency was reduced, resulting in a higher MIC of 8 µg/mL. However, variants incorporating both increased charge and hydrophobicity (WP-CAMPER1-6K5L8L and WP-CAMPER1-6K3W5W7W11W) exhibited an MIC of 4 µg/mL against S. aureus MW2, comparable to that of WP-CAMPER1. These results indicate that further enhancement of charge or hydrophobicity does not improve activity, supporting the conclusion that CAMPER selected a sequence with physicochemical properties that are near-optimal for membrane-targeting antimicrobial efficacy.

Comparison of WP-CAMPER1 with other Mastoparan peptides
To demonstrate the utility of CAMPER in identifying peptides with enhanced antimicrobial potency, we synthesized three diverse mastoparan peptides (mastoparan-S, dominulin A and mp_mastoparan) and evaluated their antimicrobial activity against S. aureus MW2, as well as their cytotoxicity in human liver-derived hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) cells and hemolysis of human red blood cells (Table S5). WP-CAMPER1 exhibited a MIC of 4 µg/mL against S. aureus MW2, while mastoparan-S (MIC= >32 µg/mL), dominulin A (MIC= 32 µg/mL) and mp_mastoparan (MIC= 32 µg/mL), showed reduced antimicrobial potencies. WP-CAMPER1 had an lethal dose 50% (LD50) of 128 µg/mL in HepG2 cells and caused 50% hemolysis at 64 µg/mL, whereas the mastoparans showed no toxicity to HepG2 cells (over 99% survival at 128 µg/mL) (Figure S6A) and < 40%, < 20% and < 10% hemolysis for dominulin A, mp_mastoparans and mastoparan-S, respectively at 128 µg/mL (Figure S6B). Although these peptides exhibit lower cytotoxicity, they show minimal or no antimicrobial activity against S. aureus MW2, limiting their relevance to CAMPER design goals and translational aims. In contrast, CAMPER enabled the design of WP-CAMPER1 from the same mastoparan scaffold, resulting in markedly superior antimicrobial potency, highlighting the utility of CAMPER in AMP design.

Potency of WP-CAMPER1 towards drug-resistant S. aureus exponential and stationary phase persister cells
To confirm the membrane-targeting and antimicrobial potential of WP-CAMPER1, we first assessed its ability to inhibit the growth of exponential-phase S. aureus strains MW2 and VRS1, before testing its efficacy against more resilient forms such as biofilms and persisters. WP-CAMPER1 rapidly suppressed the growth of exponentially growing S. aureus MW2 bacterial cells compared to control antibiotics such as gentamicin and vancomycin (Figure 3A,S7A and S8A). Whereas vancomycin was not active against S. aureus VRS1 (Figure S9A).

Subsequently, in time-kill kinetics assays, WP-CAMPER1 (40 µg/mL) eliminated 1 × 10⁸ CFU of exponential and stationary phase persister cells of S. aureus MW2 within 120 minutes of exposure (Figure 3B,C). We observed a similar result of complete cell killing within 120 mins for 1 × 106 CFU of exponential and stationary phase persister cells of S. aureus VRS1 (Figure S7B,C). WP-CAMPER1 (4 µg/mL) reduced S. aureus MW2 exponential and stationary phase persister bacterial counts by 3.2 log10 and 3.5 log10, respectively (Figure 3B,C). Under the same conditions, the control antibiotic ciprofloxacin (at 10 µg/mL) reduced S. aureus MW2 exponential cells by only 0.5 log10 and showed no activity against stationary phase persister cells, confirming the presence of a drug-tolerant persister state (Figure 3B,C). Similarly, WP-CAMPER1 (4 µg/mL) reduced S. aureus VRS1 exponential and stationary phase persister cell counts by approximately 2 log10 and 1.2 log10, respectively (Figure S7B,C). The control antibiotic linezolid (at 100 µg/mL) reduced S. aureus VRS1 exponential cells by 1.0 log10 but was inactive against the persister form of S. aureus VRS1 (Figure S7B,C). Bithionol was active against both exponential and persister populations of S. aureus MW2 and S. aureus VRS1 (Figure S8B,C and S9B,C). Compared with untreated controls, bithionol reduced the exponential-phase bacterial load by approximately 3.0 log10 CFU in S. aureus MW2 and 1.5 log10 CFU in S. aureus VRS1 (Figure S8B, S9B). In persister assays, bithionol decreased the bacterial burden by approximately 2.0 log10 CFU in S. aureus MW2 and 0.5 log10 CFU in S. aureus VRS1 (Figure S8C, S9C).

Anti-biofilm activity of WP-CAMPER1 against drug-resistant S. aureus biofilms
Next, we tested the antibiofilm activity of WP-CAMPER1 against S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 biofilms by evaluating both biofilm inhibition (Figure 3D,E and S7D,E) and disruption stages (Figure 3F,G and S7F,G). WP-CAMPER1 inhibited biofilm formation by S. aureus MW2 and VRS1, inhibited 50% of S. aureus MW2 live cells at 2 μg/mL, and reduced biofilm biomass by 50% at 6 μg/mL (MBIC50) (Figure 3D,E). For S. aureus strain VRS1, WP-CAMPER1 achieved 50% killing of live cells at 6 μg/mL and a 50% reduction in biofilm mass at 4 μg/mL (MBIC50) (Figure S7D,E). Additionally, WP-CAMPER1 disrupted 24-hour pre-established biofilm, killed 50% of live S. aureus MW2 biofilm cells and reduced biofilm biomass by 50% (MBEC50) at 12 μg/mL (Figure 3F,G). For S. aureus VRS1, WP-CAMPER1 killed 50% of biofilm-embedded cells at 16 μg/mL and reduced biofilm biomass by 50% (MBEC50) at 12 μg/mL (Figure S7F,G).

To further evaluate the antibiofilm activity of WP-CAMPER1, we included three additional S. aureus clinical isolates (BF1, BF2, and BF3) (Figure S10). WP-CAMPER1 effectively disrupted 24-hour mature biofilms formed by these isolates, achieving 50% biomass reduction (MBEC50) at 8 μg/mL, 16 μg/mL, and 12 μg/mL, respectively. Similarly, WP-CAMPER1 inhibited biofilm formation in these clinical isolates, reducing biomass by 50% (MBIC50) at 1 μg/mL (BF1), 5 μg/mL (BF2), and 3 μg/mL (BF3). These results highlight the broad-spectrum antibiofilm efficacy of WP-CAMPER1 across diverse clinical S. aureus backgrounds.

To visually assess the antibiofilm potential of WP-CAMPER1, we performed fluorescence imaging on 24-hour established S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 biofilms treated with WP-CAMPER1 (Figure 3H,I and S7H,I). Untreated control biofilms displayed predominantly SYTO9 green fluorescence (Figure 3H,S7H), indicating the presence of mostly live cells. In contrast, biofilms treated with WP-CAMPER1 (32 μg/mL) showed a pronounced propidium iodide red fluorescence, suggesting most cells were dead (Figure 3I,S7I).

We then evaluated the ability of WP-CAMPER1 to disrupt 24-hour established S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 biofilms grown on solid membrane supports (Figure 3J,S7J). WP-CAMPER1 (40 µg/mL) reduced the bacterial burden in S. aureus MW2 biofilms by 2 log10 (p=0.017) and in S. aureus VRS1 biofilms by 2.2 log10 (p=0.016)(Figure 3J,S7J), compared to the untreated control. At 4 µg/mL, WP-CAMPER1 lowered the bacterial burden by 0.3 log10 (p=0.016) for S. aureus MW2 and 1.0 log10 (p=0.024) for S. aureus VRS1 compared to the untreated control. In contrast, vancomycin at 10 μg/mL did not reduce bacterial burden in S. aureus MW2 or VRS1 strains.

Confirmation of Membrane Targeting
Because the biophysical scoring function was designed to prioritize peptides with physicochemical properties associated with membrane activity, it was essential to experimentally confirm that WP-CAMPER1, the top-ranked peptide, exerts its antimicrobial effect through direct interaction with the bacterial membrane. To this end, we conducted a series of peptide-membrane interaction studies.

To evaluate the initial membrane interaction and structural conformation of WP-CAMPER1 in a bacterial membrane-mimetic environment, we conducted circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy in the presence of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) micelles. The CD spectra exhibited characteristic minima at 208 and 222 nm, indicative of an α-helical conformation (Figure S11). Furthermore, 2D NMR spectroscopy in the presence of SDS micelles revealed that WP-CAMPER1 adopted an α-helical structure with a distinct hydrophobic surface essential for membrane interaction (Figure 4A-D). Extended structural calculations on the NMR structural restraints, hydrogen bonds, and Ramachandran plot statistics are provided in the Table S6 and Supplementary Results.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations demonstrated that WP-CAMPER1 bound to and disrupted a DOPC/DOPG(7:3) model membrane, with key residues tryptophan 1 and lysine 2, 9 and 10 forming stable hydrogen bonds and perturbing membrane integrity (Figure 4E-H). Table S7 and Supplementary Results provide details of the simulation outcomes, including hydrogen bond occupancies between DOPG/DOPC and interacting amino acids, as well as membrane water perturbation following WP-CAMPER1 insertion.

To determine whether WP-CAMPER1 could disrupt a membrane model that more closely mimics the S. aureus lipid composition, we performed MD simulations of WP-CAMPER1 with a POPG:CL (7:3) bilayer. WP-CAMPER1 rapidly associated with the membrane, binding within the first 10 ns and remaining embedded throughout the 500-ns simulation, indicating a stable and energetically favorable peptide-membrane interaction (Figure S12A). The partial density profile further demonstrated peptide insertion into the bilayer (Figure S12B).

In the next series of studies, we aimed to confirm that the membrane binding and insertion behavior of WP-CAMPER1 observed in silico reflects true membrane-targeting activity by conducting biochemical assays to assess its effects on live S. aureus MW2 cells (Figure 4I-R). Using a DiBAC4(3) fluorescence-based dye assay, we observed that WP-CAMPER1 (32 µg/mL) caused a rapid increase in fluorescence, signifying membrane depolarization (Figure 4I). Similarly, a Triton X-100 (1% v/v) control depolarized most cells, displaying maximum fluorescence intensity. Untreated bacterial cells displayed no change in DiBAC4(3) fluorescence, indicating an intact membrane potential.

As an additional test to confirm whether WP-CAMPER1 can permeabilize membranes, we performed dye permeation experiments using propidium iodide and SYTOX Green. Upon co-incubation of S. aureus MW2 cells with WP-CAMPER1 (at 4 µg/mL) and propidium iodide, we detected elevated fluorescence, suggesting WP-CAMPER1-induced membrane damage (Figure 4J). Similarly, WP-CAMPER1 (at 4 µg/mL) resulted in increased SYTOX Green fluorescence, further confirming membrane disruption (Figure 4K). Additionally, WP-CAMPER1 at 4 µg/mL led to higher ATP luminescence levels compared with untreated controls, suggesting ATP leakage due to compromised membrane integrity (Figure 4l).

To further establish the putative membrane-targeting nature of WP-CAMPER1, we employed a ΔfmtC transposon mutant from the Nebraska Transposon Mutant Library (NTML). This mutant lacks the ability to transfer a lysyl group onto the bacterial membrane surface,34 increasing its susceptibility to membrane-targeting antimicrobial agents. Compared with the wild-type background JE2 strain, WP-CAMPER1 demonstrated a two-fold reduction in MIC against the ΔfmtC mutant, suggesting enhanced membrane-disruptive activity, likely due to the reduced positive charge from the absence of lysyl transfer (Table S8).

Next, to assess the membrane-associated physiological disruptions of live S. aureus MW2 cells, we used the fluorescent probe 2′,7′-Bis-(2-carboxyethyl)-5-(and-6)-carboxyfluorescein (BCECF) to monitor changes in the ΔpH component of the proton motive force (PMF). WP-CAMPER1 at 4 μg/mL significantly perturbed ΔpH levels (Figure 4M). Additionally, WP-CAMPER1 (32 μg/mL) induced a marked increase in intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), as evidenced by enhanced fluorescence from the ROS-sensitive 2′,7′-Dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate dye (DCFH-DA) (Figure 4N).

To determine whether ROS generation directly contributed to bacterial killing as an auxiliary mechanism in addition to peptide-induced membrane disruption, we performed kinetic growth and spot-titer CFU assays in the presence of the ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine (NAC, 10 mM). In the kinetic growth assay, cultures with an initial inoculum of 1×106 CFU/mL showed a significant bacterial growth difference at 16 h when co-incubated with WP-CAMPER1 (1× MIC) and NAC (p = 0.046), whereas no growth recovery was observed in cultures treated with WP-CAMPER1 compared to untreated controls (p = 0.011) and NAC alone did not affect S. aureus MW2 growth (Figure S13A). In the spot-titer CFU assay, NAC partially restored S. aureus MW2 viability, reducing the bactericidal effect of WP-CAMPER1 by approximately 5 log10 CFU after 4 h of co-incubation (p = 0.0006), compared with the untreated control that reached 8 log10 CFU (Figure S13B). Similarly, using a higher inoculum (1×107 CFU/mL) treated with 5× MIC of WP-CAMPER1, initial bacterial killing was followed by partial regrowth in the presence of NAC, whereas complete eradication occurred with peptide treatment alone after 18 hours (Figure S13C). Together, these findings suggest that, in addition to direct membrane disruption, ROS generation contributed to the overall bactericidal mechanism of the CAMPER peptides.

To determine whether this oxidative stress led to lipid peroxidation, we employed a fluorescent based assay using C11-BODIPY dye. WP-CAMPER1 (4 μg/mL) treatment significantly increased C11-BODIPY oxidation, indicating lipid peroxidation and ROS-mediated membrane damage (Figure 4O).

Microscopic visualization of WP-CAMPER1- induced S. aureus membrane disruption
In order to visually confirm WP-CAMPER1-induced bacterial membrane damage, we employed scanning and cryo-transmission electron microscopy to examine S. aureus MW2 cells treated with the peptide WP-CAMPER1 at 40 µg/mL (Figure 4P). Untreated bacterial control cells displayed smooth and uniform surfaces, indicating intact cells (Figure 4P, upper panel). In contrast, WP-CAMPER1-treated cells exhibited prominent membrane blebbing, invaginations, and structural damage, indicating damage to bacterial membrane integrity caused by WP-CAMPER1 (Figure 4P, bottom panel). We also performed cryo-transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) on S. aureus MW2 cells treated with WP-CAMPER1 (80 µg/mL) to visualize ultrastructural changes in the bacterial membrane. Compared to the control cells (Figure 4Q, upper panel), which displayed a homogeneous and intact membrane surface, WP-CAMPER1-treated cells exhibited membrane disruption, including invaginations, vacuole-like structures, shrunken cytoplasm near the cell periphery (Figure 4Q, bottom panel), suggesting compromised membrane integrity.

Transcriptional effect of WP-CAMPER1
We performed RNA-seq analysis on WP-CAMPER1-treated S. aureus to help elucidate the mechanism by which WP-CAMPER1 impacts bacterial membrane and thus affects S. aureus persisters and biofilms. We found that treatment with WP-CAMPER1 (2 µg/mL) significantly altered gene expression, causing 852 upregulated and 843 downregulated genes (p < 0.05) (Supplementary Data 2,3). Notably, WP-CAMPER1 significantly affected the expression of S. aureus pathways involved in bacterial virulence, oxidative phosphorylation, folate biosynthesis, and energy metabolism (Figure 4R). These transcriptional changes reflect bacterial stress responses to WP-CAMPER1 and support our hypothesis that CAMPER-designed peptides selectively disrupt membrane integrity while triggering broader physiological effects. Detailed analysis of gene expression changes across multiple regulatory pathways is provided in the Supplementary Results.

In vivo therapeutic efficacy of WP-CAMPER1 on a murine skin infection model
To evaluate whether the bacterial membrane-targeting activity of WP-CAMPER1 translates into protective efficacy in vivo, we next tested its ability to reduce bacterial burden in a skin infection model that mimics early-stage or prophylactic intervention. We employed an abraded murine skin infection model, infecting mice with 107 CFU of S. aureus MW2 to evaluate the in vivo efficacy of WP-CAMPER1 (Figure 5A). A single application of the 2% (w/w) WP-CAMPER1 formulation, administered 10 minutes after infection (representing a prophylactic model), led to a significant reduction in S. aureus MW2 bacterial load (evaluated after 24 h), achieving a 2.5 log10 decrease (p = 0.0002) (95% CI = 2.15 – 2.85) compared to the vehicle treated mice groups (Figure 5B). The 1% (w/w) formulation also demonstrated efficacy, reducing the bacterial load by 1.4 log10 (p = 0.0005) (95% CI = 0.84 – 1.42). As a positive control, mupirocin ointment (2% w/w) resulted in a 2.2 log10 reduction in S. aureus MW2 burden (p = 0.0002) (95% CI = 1.82 – 2.48) compared to the vehicle treated mice. In addition to decreased bacterial burden, the skin of mice treated with the WP-CAMPER1 (2% w/w) formulation exhibited significantly lower levels of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines compared to the vehicle treated skin, including TNF-α (14-fold reduction, p=0.029), IL-1β (4-fold, p=0.028), IFN-γ (2.2-fold, p=0.004), MCP-1 (2-fold, p=0.023), and IL-6 (5-fold, p=0.002) (Figure S14).

Class A peptidomimetics of WP-CAMPER1
After confirming the membrane-targeting mechanism, in vitro potency, and topical efficacy of WP-CAMPER1, we sought to explore its efficacy in a murine thigh infection model of persistent S. aureus, which involves systemic administration of the study agent. Because WP-CAMPER1, like other α-helical peptides could be vulnerable to enzymatic degradation by host and bacterial proteases,14 we hypothesized that its D-enantiomeric variant could retain comparable antimicrobial activity, due to preservation of the key physicochemical properties prioritized by CAMPER (charge, hydrophobicity, helicity, and amphipathicity), while offering resistance to proteolytic degradation.

We synthesized WP-CAMPER1-d alongside a set of Class A peptidomimetics that preserve the overall peptide backbone structure of WP-CAMPER1 but incorporate substitutions at lysine residues with non-proteinogenic amino acids to avoid recognition and degradation by proteases. We evaluated the resulting peptide variants for activity against a panel of antibiotic-resistant S. aureus strains (Table 2). As hypothesized, WP-CAMPER1-d retained antimicrobial activity comparable to that of the parent peptide WP-CAMPER1 (4–8 μg/mL), mirroring the intact physicochemical profile prioritized by CAMPER. In contrast, analogs containing diaminobutyric acid (Dab), diaminopimelic acid (Dap), and ornithine (Orn) substitutions, which disrupted the physicochemical properties prioritized by CAMPER, showed reduced potency (MIC 8–32 μg/mL), and the cyclic variant was inactive (MIC > 32 μg/mL).

Next, we tested the stability of WP-CAMPER1-d to α-chymotrypsin and its cytotoxicity against various human cell lines. WP-CAMPER1-d remained intact after 24 hours of α-chymotrypsin exposure, whereas linear WP-CAMPER1 was fully degraded within 2 hours (Figure S15). Hemolysis assays showed comparable toxicity (Figure S16). Against other human cell lines, the LD50 of WP-CAMPER1 was 120 µg/mL in HaCaT, 128 µg/mL in HepG2, and 55 µg/mL in HKC-8 cells. For WP-CAMPER1-d, the LD50 values were 65 µg/mL in HaCaT, 50 µg/mL in HepG2, and 35 µg/mL in HKC-8 cells (Figure S17). Overall, WP-CAMPER1-d exhibited a promising anti-staphylococcal profile compared to other lysin substituted peptidomimetics, showed proteolytic stability and a defined therapeutic window.

We also evaluated whether S. aureus MW2 could develop resistance to WP-CAMPER1 and WP-CAMPER1-d. No resistance was observed after 21 serial passages, as MIC values remained unchanged (Figure 5C). In contrast, ciprofloxacin exhibited a >4-fold MIC increase by day 15 and a >16-fold increase by day 21, indicating the emergence of resistance.

To assess the persistence of bacterial growth suppression following peptide exposure, we evaluated the post-antibiotic effect (PAE) of WP-CAMPER1 and WP-CAMPER1-d against S. aureus MW2. The PAE values for WP-CAMPER1, WP-CAMPER1-d, and ciprofloxacin, relative to the untreated control, were 1.68 ± 0.19 h (95% CI= 1.26–2.10) (p= 0.0009), 2.45 ± 0.31 h (95% CI= 1.67–3.23) (p < 0.0001), and 0.91 ± 0.17 h (95% CI= 0.53–1.29) (p= 0.0047), respectively. Notably, the PAE of WP-CAMPER1-d was significantly longer than that of WP-CAMPER1 (p = 0.018), confirming that D-enantiomerization prolongs post-antibiotic suppression relative to the parent peptide. These findings demonstrate that both CAMPER-derived peptides exhibit prolonged bacterial growth inhibition compared with ciprofloxacin, with WP-CAMPER1-d showing the strongest and most durable effect.

Anti-persister activity of WP-CAMPER1-d against exponential phase S. aureus persisters
To assess ability of WP-CAMPER1 and WP-CAMPER1-d against persisters cells in an environment that is closer to the in vivo conditions, we used the Mother Machine, a single-cell microfluidic assay. Using this platform, we monitored ~5,520 trenches, each containing ~20 exponential-phase S. aureus USA300 cells, and exposed them to a bactericidal concentration of gentamicin (3.75 µg/mL) (Figure 5D,E). During first gentamicin treatment, out of 5,520 trenches analyzed across four biological replicates, only 4 trenches contained surviving lineages after treatment with survival frequency: (4/5520, 0.072%; 95% CI: 0.019% to 0.185%), exhibiting a persister-like phenotype (Figure 5D). These results correspond to a survival frequency of 0.069% based on lineage-level analysis. However, during the second gentamicin treatment (3.75 µg/mL) in which, the four surviving lineages from the first gentamicin treatment were exposed to a second challenge: two each for retreatment with gentamicin or with the WP-CAMPER1-d peptide (60 µg/mL) (Figure 5D) (Supplementary Video 1). In gentamicin retreatment: both lineages survived (2/2, 100%; 95% CI: 15.811%–100%) (Supplementary Video 2,3), while during peptide retreatment with WP-CAMPER1-d, both lineages were eradicated (0/2, 0%; 95% CI: 0%–84.188%) (Supplementary Video 4,5), indicating a differential response to the two treatment regimens (Figure 5D,E).

In vivo efficacy of WP-CAMPER1-d in a murine biofilm and a persister infection model
Following the single-cell evidence of anti-persister activity of WP-CAMPER1-d against exponential-phase MRSA persisters, we sought to evaluate its efficacy in capturing both surface-associated and deep-tissue infections. We employed two murine infection models: a biofilm-associated skin infection and a deep-seated thigh infection model (Figure 5F,H). In the established biofilm model, a single topical dose of WP-CAMPER1-d (2% w/w in white petroleum jelly), applied 24 hours post-infection, significantly reduced S. aureus MW2 burden by 1.37 log10 CFU (p < 0.0001) (95% CI = 0.90–1.84) compared to the vehicle treated animal group (Figure 5G). In comparison, WP-CAMPER1 (2% w/w) reduced the bacterial load by 1.22 log10 CFU (p < 0.0001) (95% CI = 0.73–1.71), which was only 0.15 log10 CFU lower than WP-CAMPER1-d, indicating similar efficacy between L- and D- forms of WP-CAMPER1, since the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.496). Meanwhile the 2% mupirocin ointment control achieved a reduction of 2.06 log10 CFU (p < 0.0001) (95% CI = 1.54–2.58) compared to the control mice treated with white petroleum jelly (Figure 5G). Bacterial reduction by mupirocin was 0.69 log10 CFU (p = 0.0198) (95% CI = 0.13–1.26) greater than that achieved by WP-CAMPER1-d and approximately 0.84 log10 CFU (p = 0.0080) (95% CI = 0.26–1.42) greater than WP-CAMPER1.

In the deep-seated thigh infection model, WP-CAMPER1-d (10 mg/Kg) reduced the bacterial load of stationary-phase S. aureus MW2 persister cells by 1.6 log10 CFU (p < 0.0001) (95% CI: 1.33–1.87), whereas WP-CAMPER1 achieved a 1.05 log10 reduction (p < 0.001) (95% CI = 0.81–1.29), compared to the vehicle treated animal group (Figure 5I). The observed additional ~0.55 log10 reduction in S. aureus MW2 burden with WP-CAMPER1-d compared to WP-CAMPER1 (p = 0.0029), suggests that the enhanced enzymatic stability of the D-form may play a critical role, ultimately affecting the extent of bacterial clearance. In contrast, treatment with the control antibiotic vancomycin (30 mg/Kg) was ineffective, confirming the presence of antibiotic-tolerant persisters and validating the bacterial persistence in the deep-seated thigh infection model. We also evaluated the renal toxicity of WP-CAMPER1-d and WP-CAMPER1 by measuring serum levels of blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Neither WP-CAMPER1 nor WPCAMPER1-d led to a statistically significant increase in BUN levels compared to the vehicle-treated control group (Figure S18).
