## Methods

Approvals
All animal studies were performed in accordance with all relevant ethical regulations and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Houston Methodist Research Institute (Houston, Texas, USA; protocol numbers IS00008777 and IS00008451).

Data Collection and Preprocessing
We collected peptide sequences with MIC measurements against Staphylococcus aureus from the Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) (https://dbaasp.org/)68 and converted all sequences to uppercase and removed duplicates to maintain consistency. We excluded sequences containing non-standard amino acid symbols. Specifically, we removed sequences that included X (any amino acid, unknown, or unspecified), B (asparagine or aspartic acid, ambiguous), Z (glutamine or glutamic acid, ambiguous), J (leucine or isoleucine, ambiguous), U (selenocysteine), and O (pyrrolysine).

In data preprocessing, we labeled peptides with MIC values of 32 µg/mL or lower as active and those with MIC values of 64 µg/mL or greater as inactive, excluding peptides with MIC values between 32 and 64 µg/mL. This binning strategy was selected to support the primary goal of CAMPER, which is to identify high-confidence peptide candidates with strong activity. MIC values between 32 and 64 µg/mL often fall into an ambiguous range that can vary by experimental conditions and including them can introduce label noise. Broth MIC measurements commonly vary by approximately one two-fold dilution, so values that differ by a single dilution step fall within expected assay variability.69 Because our aim was to design a selective prioritization tool to maximize precision and reduce the number of non-active peptides forwarded for synthesis and testing, we used conservative thresholds to retain only peptides with clear activity or clear inactivity. For peptides with multiple MIC measurements, we averaged their binary activity labels (0 for inactive, 1 for active) and classified peptides with a mean activity score greater than 0.5 as active, reflecting a predominance of active measurements.

Feature Engineering
We evaluated three feature-engineering strategies to characterize peptide sequences: Physicochemical descriptors and fingerprints. To calculate peptide descriptors, we used the RDKit70 (version 2023.03.3) and Biopython71 (version 1.83) libraries (Python 3.11.3). We computed a comprehensive set of physicochemical descriptors,72 including Grand Average of Hydropathy (GRAVY), helicity, hydrophobic moment, charge, topological polar surface area (TPSA), LogP, fraction of sp3 carbons, molar refractivity, hydrogen bond donors and acceptors, molecular weight, partial charges, aromatic ring count, and various Chi and Kappa indices.73 We added each descriptor as a feature in the dataset (Table S1). Additionally, we calculated Morgan fingerprints (2048-bit, radius 4) to represent substructure features in a binary vector format.74 A detailed rationale for the relevance of each descriptor class to peptide biophysics and antimicrobial activity is provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Sequence n-grams: We generated k-mer frequency vectors from the primary amino-acid sequence to capture short-range compositional patterns. We evaluated several n-gram sizes and normalized counts before model training.

ProtBERT embeddings: We extracted contextual embeddings for each peptide using the ProtBERT language model.75 We averaged token embeddings to produce a fixed-length representation of each sequence, which we used directly as input to downstream classifiers.

Model Training and Evaluation
We created a stratified 80 to 20 outer split, reserving the 20% portion as a fixed external holdout set. We used the remaining 80% of the data for model development and evaluation. We trained a random forest classifier and optimized model performance using 5-fold cross validation to select the best-performing hyperparameters. Random forest is an ensemble learning method that constructs multiple decision trees during training and outputs the class that is the majority vote among the trees, enhancing accuracy and reducing overfitting.76 To compare performance with other commonly used classifiers, we trained XGBoost77, and logistic regression with L1 Regularization (Lasso)78 classifiers (using scikit-learn version 1.5.2) on each feature-engineering strategy described in the feature engineering section of the Methods.

To prevent near-duplicate sequences from leaking across folds, we applied homology-aware 5-fold cross-validation inside the 80% training set. We computed pairwise sequence identity using the Levenshtein ratio,79 clustered peptides at the chosen identity threshold, and assigned entire clusters to the same fold. This approach ensured that homologous peptides did not appear on opposite sides of a training–validation split. To identify an appropriate sequence-identity threshold, we performed a sensitivity analysis in which we repeated the clustering and homology-aware cross-validation across multiple similarity cutoffs and compared both the resulting cluster structure and performance metrics of the RF classifier at each threshold.

We computed accuracy, precision, recall (also known as sensitivity), and F1-score to assess predictive performance. In the following formulas, TP is the number of true positives, TN is the number of true negatives, FP is the number of false positives, and FN is the number of false negatives.

Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly classified instances out of the total instances and is defined as:
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) (1)

Precision indicates the proportion of true positive predictions among all positive predictions, providing insight into the model’s accuracy for the positive class:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) (2)

Recall (sensitivity), measures the proportion of actual positive instances that the model correctly identifies:
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) (3)

The F1-score, which is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, provides a balance between the two and is especially useful when classes are imbalanced:
F1 Score = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall) (4)

These metrics offer a comprehensive assessment of the model’s predictive performance, considering both its overall accuracy and its effectiveness in correctly classifying positive cases and making reliable positive predictions.

To assess model robustness, we performed y-randomization80 by randomly shuffling the response variable (active/inactive) in the training dataset while keeping the feature variables unchanged. We repeated this process 100 times, evaluating model performance after each iteration. Comparing the performance of the original model to these randomized models allowed us to assess whether the observed accuracy was likely due to meaningful patterns in the data rather than random chance.

CAMPER (Constraint-driven AMP Engineering with Ranking)
To enhance the prediction of antimicrobial activity against S. aureus, we developed CAMPER (Constraint-driven AMP Engineering with Ranking), a hybrid framework that combines the RF model with a mechanistic biophysical scoring function that incorporates key physicochemical determinants of peptide-membrane interactions. This approach extended the ML model beyond statistical pattern recognition by explicitly modeling the mechanistic basis of antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria. Four critical physicochemical properties were selected based on their established roles in antimicrobial peptide (AMP) function:

Charge. Net positive charge is essential for initial electrostatic attraction to the negatively charged bacterial surface of S. aureus, which contains teichoic acids and negatively charged phospholipids such as phosphatidylglycerol.8 Unlike mammalian cell membranes, which are primarily zwitterionic, the negative charge density of Gram-positive bacterial surfaces creates a selective targeting mechanism for cationic peptides. However, excessive cationic character can potentially prevent membrane insertion by creating overly strong surface interactions and trap the peptide at the membrane surface, preventing deeper insertion and pore formation.8,11 Thus, membrane-active peptides require a specific range of positive charge for optimal activity, with both insufficient and excessive charge reducing effectiveness.14 We modeled this range with a Gaussian function:
ChargeScore = exp(-(q - q_opt)^2 / (2 * sigma^2)) (5)
Where:
• q is the peptide’s net charge.
• q_opt is the optimal charge
• sigma is the width parameter that determines how quickly the score decreases as charge deviates from q_optimal.
This function produces a maximum value of 1.0 when q= q_opt and decreases symmetrically as charge moves away from optimal in either direction, capturing the domain knowledge that both insufficient and excessive charge reduce antimicrobial effectiveness.

Helicity. The ability to form helical structures upon membrane contact is a crucial determinant of antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, including S. aureus.47 This structural transition typically occurs at the bacterial membrane interface and enables the peptide to organize its amino acids into an amphipathic arrangement. Structure-activity relationship studies demonstrate that peptides with helicity below a critical threshold fail to adopt the necessary conformation for membrane disruption, resulting in substantially reduced antibacterial activity.24,47 This suggests a non-linear, threshold-dependent relationship between helicity and antimicrobial potency. We modeled this threshold effect using a sigmoid function:
HelicityScore = 1 / (1 + exp(-k_h * (h - h_threshold))) (6)
Where:
• h is the peptide’s helical propensity (0 to 1 scale).
• h_threshold is the inflection point where activity begins to increase rapidly
• k_h is the steepness parameter that controls how rapidly the function transitions from low to high values.
The sigmoid function produces a smooth S-shaped curve that maps helicity to a score between 0 and 1. When helicity is well below the threshold (h ≪ h_threshold), the score approaches 0. As helicity increases and crosses the threshold, the score rises rapidly, eventually approaching 1 as helicity becomes sufficiently high (h ≫ h_threshold). This formulation reflects the understanding that increased helicity improves the likelihood of stable membrane interaction, supporting the peptide’s ability to insert and disrupt the bilayer.81

Hydrophobicity. Gram-positive bacterial membranes contain a higher proportion of branched-chain fatty acids compared to mammalian membranes, creating distinct hydrophobic environments.8 Sufficient hydrophobicity, measured by the Grand Average of Hydropathy (GRAVY), is essential for peptide insertion into these membrane environments. AMPs with higher hydrophobicity values can penetrate deeper into the hydrophobic core of the bacterial membrane.82 Similar to helicity, hydrophobicity exhibits a threshold-dependent effect, where values below a certain level prevent effective membrane insertion regardless of other properties.82 We modeled this using another sigmoid function:
GravyScore = 1 / (1 + exp(-k_g * (G - G_threshold))) (7)
Where:
• G is the GRAVY value of the peptide.
• G_threshold is the minimum effective GRAVY value.
• k_g is the steepness parameter controlling the transition rate.
This mathematical representation aligns with biophysical evidence that peptides must achieve sufficient hydrophobicity to overcome the energetic barrier of inserting into the lipid bilayer.

Amphipathicity. The spatial segregation of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues, quantified by the hydrophobic moment (μ_H), enables peptides to simultaneously interact with both the polar headgroups and hydrophobic core of bacterial membranes.24 For Gram-positive targets such as S. aureus, where peptidoglycan layers may partially shield membranes, strong amphipathicity facilitates deeper penetration and subsequent membrane disruption.8 This property mediates multiple mechanisms of action including barrel-stave, toroidal pore, and carpet models of membrane permeabilization,8 each requiring a minimum threshold of amphipathicity to be effective. We modeled this using a sigmoid function:
AmphipathicityScore = 1 / (1 + exp(-k_a * (μ_H - μ_H,threshold))) (8)
Where:
• μ_H is the hydrophobic moment, measuring the segregation of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues.
• μ_H,threshold is the minimum effective hydrophobic moment.
• k_a is the steepness parameter controlling the transition rate.
Like the other sigmoid functions, this mathematical formulation produces a score that transitions from near-zero to near-one as the amphipathicity crosses the threshold value. This function models the biophysical requirement for sufficient segregation of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues to interact effectively with bacterial membranes.

Membrane-active peptides operate through a multi-step mechanism involving initial electrostatic binding to membrane surfaces, hydrophobic insertion into the lipid bilayer, and subsequent pore formation or membrane permeabilization.82 Each step requires simultaneous contribution from multiple physicochemical properties: charge facilitates initial membrane binding and selectivity, hydrophobicity drives insertion into the lipid core, helicity ensures proper orientation and depth, and amphipathicity interfacial alignment and peptide clustering.8,11,24,81 This creates interdependencies where deficiency in one property cannot be compensated by excess in others, as each step requires a minimum threshold of all relevant properties to proceed effectively. We mathematically model this cooperative nature through two mechanisms:

Cooperative Effect (Minimum Function). The minimum function captures the rate-limiting step concept in peptide-membrane interactions:
CooperativeEffect = min(ChargeScore, HelicityScore, GravyScore, AmphipathicityScore) (9)
This function returns the lowest value among all input scores, imposing a strict constraint that the overall effectiveness cannot exceed that of the weakest component. This reflects the sequential, multi-step nature of peptide-membrane interactions, where deficiency in any step creates a bottleneck for the entire process.

Cooperative Boost (Threshold Function). We also implemented a threshold-based cooperative boost that captures the synergistic enhancement observed when all properties exceed minimum requirements:
CooperativeBoost = β * I(all scores > τ) (10)
Where:
• β is the boost magnitude.
• τ is the quality threshold.
• I(⋅) is the indicator function that equals 1 when the condition is satisfied and 0 otherwise.
This creates a step function that adds a constant bonus (β) when all component scores exceed the threshold τ and contributes nothing otherwise.

Final Score Calculation. The component scores were combined into a comprehensive biophysical score, which was then normalized and integrated with the ML prediction:
RawBiophysicalScore = ∑(w_i * Component_i) + CooperativeBoost (11)
Where w_i are the component weights for each property and cooperative term.
To ensure the biophysical score remains within the [0,1] range for consistent interpretation, we apply normalization:
BiophysicalScore = RawBiophysicalScore / (∑ w_i + β) (12)
We combined the ML probability and the biophysical score using a simple weighted sum to generate the final CAMPER score:
FinalScore = w_prob * MLProbability + (1 - w_prob) * BiophysicalScore (13)
Where w_prob controls the balance between data-driven and mechanism-based predictions.

Optimization of the Biophysical Scoring Function
To define meaningful threshold values for the biophysical scoring function, we utilized peptide sequences from the Antimicrobial Peptide Database (APD) (https://aps.unmc.edu/) that were active against Gram-positive bacteria and experimentally confirmed to adopt an α-helical structure.83 For each of the four biophysical features used in the scorer (net charge, predicted helicity, hydrophobicity, and amphipathicity) we calculated the median value across this curated set. These medians were then used as the threshold parameters in the transformation functions previously defined (sigmoid for helicity, hydrophobicity, and amphipathicity; Gaussian for charge).

We then performed a grid search with five-fold cross-validation to tune the remaining hyperparameters of the scoring function. This included the steepness of the transformation functions, a threshold and weight controlling the contribution of cooperative effects between features, individual weights for each biophysical component, and a mixing weight that balances the biophysical score with the predicted probability of the random forest model. Cross-validation was conducted exclusively on the training set of the random forest classifier, ensuring that the test set remained untouched during parameter selection. For each hyperparameter combination, a biophysical scorer was fit to the training folds and applied to the validation fold. Performance was evaluated using ranking metrics, with precision in the top 10% of ranked peptides as the primary optimization target. The best-performing parameter set was selected based on the average cross-validated performance across all folds.

Precision Analysis Across Biophysical Property Space
To evaluate how prediction precision varied across key biophysical properties, we conducted a stratified analysis of test set performance for the RF model and CAMPER. For each property, GRAVY, helicity, net charge, and hydrophobic moment the test set was divided into eight equal-width bins spanning the observed range. Bins with fewer than 10 samples were excluded to ensure statistical robustness.
Within each bin, we calculated precision for both the RF model and the biophysically adjusted predictions. We then computed the absolute improvement in precision introduced by the biophysical adjustment. These values were used to identify regions of the property space where the biophysical integration improved prediction reliability.

Rational Design of a Peptide Pool Library
To demonstrate the ability of CAMPER to prioritize potent, membrane-active AMPs, we applied the pipeline to a candidate pool derived from a natural 14-mer template, using it as a proof of concept for targeted in silico screening. To generate the pool, we selected a mastoparan template, a 14-mer natural peptide from the wasp family, a group of amphipathic, cationic α-helical peptides found in the venom of insects of the Hymenoptera order.84 While CAMPER can be applied to any linear peptide sequence to enhance peptide-membrane interact through ideal amino acid substitutions, we selected this peptide template because it exhibited a distinct pattern of conserved and non-conserved amino acid positions (Figure S19). We specifically targeted the non-conserved residues, as they were not restricted to any specific class of amino acids and could either contribute to increased net charge for electrostatic interactions or participate in hydrophobic interactions with the membrane.

While linear peptides of various lengths can be used, shorter AMP sequences are generally more cost-effective for therapeutic applications.11 Therefore, we first optimized the sequence by removing amino acids that were unlikely to contribute to bacterial membrane binding. Specifically, to shorten the mastoparan peptide, we removed the first two N-terminal residues, isoleucine and asparagine, since they do not participate in the α-helical structure, as shown by the NMR structure of mastoparan-L in detergent micelles mimicking bacterial membranes (PDB ID: 1D7N),85 and thus are not involved in membrane interactions critical for peptide activity (Figure S20). This truncation yielded a 12-residue peptide template retaining three helical turns.

Next, we determined which amino acid positions in this 12-residue template could be substituted to enhance its antimicrobial potential. We aligned all known mastoparan peptide sequences to identify conserved and non-conserved amino acid positions (Figure S19). The sequence of our 12-residue wasp derived (WP) template was (WKXIAXXAKKXL), where X represents the non-conserved residues (positions 3, 6, 7, and 11) (Figure S19). We substituted these four positions with all possible amino acid combinations, generating a pool of 160,000 (20^4) peptides.

Validation of WP-CAMPER1 by traditional quantitative-structure activity relationship (QSAR)-based peptide design
To assess whether CAMPER successfully prioritized peptide sequences with charge, hydrophobicity, and amphipathicity profiles optimized for membrane-disruptive antimicrobial activity, we conducted a QSAR analysis of WP-CAMPER1, the top-scoring peptide from the CAMPER screen. This involved introducing targeted substitutions of hydrophilic and hydrophobic residues on distinct helical faces of the peptide to evaluate how changes in physicochemical properties affected antimicrobial potency. To assess the effect of increasing charge, we replaced leucine (non-conserved position) at position 6 on the hydrophilic face with lysine, creating WP-CAMPER1-6K. To enhance the hydrophobicity of this charged variant, we substituted alanine residues (conserved positions) at positions 5 and 8 with leucine, generating WP-CAMPER1-6K5L8L. To further increase the hydrophobicity of WP-CAMPER1-6K, we substituted tryptophan residues at positions 3, 7, and 11 (non-conserved positions) to generate WP-CAMPER1-6K3W7W11W and at positions 3, 5, 7, 8, and 11 (all hydrophobic positions) to produce WP-CAMPER1-6K3W5W7W11W. Finally, we enhanced the hydrophobicity of the hydrophobic face while keeping the overall charge of the ML-selected peptide unchanged. Starting with WP-CAMPER1 we replaced the alanine (conserved positions) at positions 5 and 8 with leucine, resulting in WP-CAMPER1-5L8L.

Bacterial strains growth conditions and peptide synthesis
We employed a panel of S. aureus strains exhibiting diverse antibiotic susceptibility profiles, as detailed in Table S9. All S. aureus strains were grown in tryptic soy broth (TSB) (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) under standard aerobic conditions at 37°C with shaking unless otherwise stated.

Synthesis of peptides
We synthesized the peptides using solid-phase chemistry (GenScript Inc., Piscataway, NJ, USA). These peptides had a purity of 95% or higher (List of peptides and their characterization data can be found in Figure S21).

Minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) assay
We determined the MIC of candidate peptides using the broth microdilution method described by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute.86 We prepared serial dilutions of 10× concentrated peptides (10 µL) in duplicate in 96-well plates (Cat no. 3595, Corning, NY, USA). To these dilutions, we added 90 µL of logarithmic-phase bacteria at 1 × 106 CFU/mL (in TSB) and incubated the plates at 37°C for 18 hours. We then measured AOD600 on a Spectra Max i3x spectrophotometer (Molecular Devices, CA, USA) and determined the MIC as the lowest concentration of peptides that completely inhibited bacterial growth. To assess peptide activity under various salt conditions, we incorporated physiologically relevant concentrations of salts and serum into the TSB medium, adding 150 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM CaCl2, 8 µM ZnSO4, 1 mM MgSO4, and 5-10% human serum to medium for MIC assays.

S. aureus persister cell and time-kill assays
We generated antibiotic-induced S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 persister cells by following an established protocol.87 We grew 25 ml cultures of S. aureus strains MW2 and VRS1 to stationary phase, then treated the cells with gentamicin at 20 μg/mL for an additional 4 hours. After washing the bacterial cultures three times with 25 ml of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), we adjusted the cultures to ~1 × 108 CFU/mL for S. aureus MW2 and ~1 × 107 CFU/mL for S. aureus VRS1 in PBS. To assess the killing kinetics of WP-CAMPER1 in persister cells, we added 1 mL of cell suspension to wells in a 2-ml deep-well assay block (Cat no. 3960, Corning, NY, USA) containing 10× MIC or 1× MIC of the peptide. We also included ciprofloxacin (at 10 μg/mL) for S. aureus MW2 and linezolid (100 μg/mL) for S. aureus VRS1 as antibiotic controls. We incubated the plates at 37°C with shaking at 225 rpm. At specific time points (0, 15, 30, 60, and 120 minutes), we collected 10 μL samples, performed serial dilutions, and plated them on tryptic soy agar (TSA) (BD Difco, NJ, USA) plates. The TSA plates were incubated at 37°C for 18 hours, and then we counted resulting colonies. We conducted these experiments in duplicate. For comparison, we prepared exponential-phase cells of S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 in PBS and analyzed their killing kinetics in the same way as described for persister cells.

Biofilm viability assay on solid support
We generated gentamicin-induced S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 persister cells as outlined above. Afterward, we diluted the persister cell culture 1:200 in TSB medium supplemented with 0.2% glucose.88 To form biofilms on substrates, we applied 1 ml of diluted bacterial culture onto a 13-mm Millipore mixed cellulose ester membrane (Cat no. HAWP01300, Millipore, MA, USA) at the bottom of a 12-well plate (Cat no. 353043, Falcon, MA, USA) and incubated it statically at 37°C for 24 hours. After incubation, we removed the planktonic cells by washing the membranes twice and transferred them to a fresh 12-well plate. We then added 1 ml of PBS containing 10× MIC concentrations of peptides and antibiotics to each well and incubated the plates under static conditions at 37°C for another 24 hours. Following this, we washed the membranes twice with PBS, placed them in 1 ml of PBS, and sonicated them in an FS 30 ultrasonic bath (Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) for 10 minutes. The sonicated samples were serially diluted with PBS in a 96-well plate, spot-plated onto TSA plates, and incubated overnight at 37°C. The following day, we counted the viable bacterial colonies.

Prevention of S. aureus biofilm formation
We assessed the ability of the designed wasp-derived peptides to inhibit biofilm formation using an established protocol with minor modifications.87 Briefly, we grew exponential cultures of S. aureus MW2 and VRS1, adjusted to OD600 = 0.01, in TSB medium supplemented with 0.2% glucose, starting from overnight cultures. We then added 90 µL of this bacterial culture to 10 µL of serially diluted 10× peptide solutions in flat-bottomed 96-well polystyrene microtiter plates (Cat no. Corning 3595, NY, USA) and incubated the plates at 37°C for 24 hours. TSB medium containing bacteria with water served as the positive control, while TSB medium with sterile water acted as the negative control. After incubation, we carefully removed the TSB medium and washed the wells with PBS (Gibco, MD, USA) to eliminate loosely attached planktonic cells. We stained the biofilms with crystal violet to quantify the biomass and determined the concentration of peptide that inhibited 50% of biofilm formation (MBIC50). To measure the live-cell count within the biofilms, we used XTT dye [2,3-bis(2-methyloxy-4-nitro-5-sulfophenyl)-2H-tertazolium-5-carboxanilide] (ATCC, VA, USA). The percentage of biofilm growth was calculated by normalizing the biofilm growth in peptide-treated wells to that in wells containing untreated bacteria.89

Disruption of S. aureus established biofilms
We evaluated the ability of the designed peptides to disrupt established biofilms following an established protocol with modifications.87 We prepared exponential cultures of S. aureus MW2 and VRS1 and adjusted to 1 × 106 CFU/mL in TSB medium supplemented with 0.2% glucose from overnight cultures. We then added 100 µL of this bacterial culture to flat-bottomed 96-well polystyrene microtiter plates (Cat no. 3595, Corning, NY, USA) and incubated the plates statically at 37°C for 24 hours to allow biofilm formation. After incubation, we carefully removed the TSB medium and gently washed the wells with PBS (Gibco, MD, USA) to eliminate loosely attached planktonic cells. We treated the established biofilms with 10 µL of serially diluted 10× peptide solutions and added 90 µL of TSB medium supplemented with 0.2% glucose to each well. The plates were incubated for an additional 24 hours at 37°C before processing the biomass and live-cell content. We then calculated the concentration of peptide required to disrupt 50% of the established biofilms (MBEC50).

Fluorescence microscopy of WP-CAMPER1-treated S. aureus established biofilms
We performed fluorescence microscopy on WP-CAMPER1-treated S. aureus biofilms using a previously described protocol with modifications.24 In brief, we prepared exponential-phase cultures of S. aureus MW2 and VRS1, adjusting the bacterial count to 1 × 106 CFU/mL in fresh TSB medium. To establish biofilms, we added 200 µL of the bacterial culture to the chambers of Millicell EZ Slides (Millipore Sigma, MA, USA) and incubated them statically at 37°C for 24 hours. After incubation, we carefully removed the TSB medium and gently washed the Millicell wells with PBS (Gibco, MD, USA) to eliminate loosely attached planktonic cells. We then treated the established biofilms with 20 µL of WP-CAMPER1 peptide (at 10× MIC) and added 180 µL of TSB medium. The Millicell slides were incubated for an additional 24 hours at 37°C. Following this, we gently washed the Millicell slides with PBS to remove planktonic cells and stained the biofilms with 50 µL of staining reagent from a LIVE/DEAD kit (Life Technologies, OR, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We visualized the biofilms using a Nikon ECLIPSE Ti fluorescent microscope (Melville, NY, USA) and processed the images with NIS-Elements AR 4.00.07 software (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan).

Mammalian cell cytotoxicity assays
We assessed the ability of the peptides to induce hemoglobin leakage in human red blood cells using a previously established method.90 First, we washed human erythrocytes (Rockland Immunochemicals, PA, USA) three times with an equal volume of PBS and resuspended them in a 4% solution. We then added 100 µL of this cell suspension to 100 µL of a 2× peptide solution in a 96-well microtiter plate (Cat no. 3595, Corning, NY, USA) and incubated the plates at 37°C for 1 hour. Following incubation, we centrifuged the plates at 500× g for 5 minutes, transferred 100 µL of the supernatant to a new 96-well plate, and measured the absorbance at 540 nm. We calculated the percent hemolysis using the formula: (A540 nm of peptide solution − A540 nm of PBS) / (A540 nm of 1% Triton X-100 − A540 nm of PBS) × 100, where 100% hemolysis was defined by 1% Triton X-100 and 0% hemolysis was defined by PBS.

We used liver-derived HepG2 cells (Cat. No. HB-8065, American Type Culture Collection, Manassas, VA, USA), human keratinocytes (HaCaT) (Cat. No. T0020001, Fisher Scientific, MA, USA), and human kidney cortical (HKC-8) cells (courtesy of Dr. Racusen of John Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD) to evaluate the cytotoxicity of AMP based on an established protocol.90 We cultured HepG2, HaCaT, and HKC-8 cells at 37°C with 5% CO2 in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco, MA, USA). At ~85% confluence, cells were harvested, resuspended in fresh DMEM medium and seeded at 1 x 106 cells/well in a 96-well plate (Cat no. 3598, Corning, NY, USA) for 24 h at 37°C with 5% CO2. Cells were subsequently treated with 100 μL two-fold serially diluted peptides in DMEM for an additional 24 h. After treatment, 70 μL of the XTT-electron coupling reagent mixture (CyQUANT™ XTT cell viability assay kit (Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) was added to each well and incubated for 4 h. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm and 660 nm using the SpectraMax 250 plate reader (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA).

Circular dichroism (CD)
We recorded the CD spectra of WP-CAMPER1 (0.2 mg/mL) in the presence and absence of 50 mM sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) using a Jasco J-815 Circular Dichroism (CD) Spectropolarimeter (Jasco, OK, USA) according to a previously described method.91 We placed the samples in a thermostat cell holder set to 25°C, using a quartz cell with a 1-mm path length. The CD data were expressed as mean residue ellipticity. We obtained baseline scans under the same conditions for samples containing only buffer, micelles, and vesicles, and subtracted these baseline scans from the data obtained with peptide-containing samples.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)
We investigated the membrane-targeting mechanism of WP-CAMPER1 using two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (2D-NMR) spectroscopy, following a previously published method with minor modifications.59 We collected the NMR data at 25ºC on a Bruker Avance II 500 MHz NMR spectrometer (Bruker, MA, USA), using 600 µL of 2 mM WP-CAMPER1 dissolved in 80 mM deuterated SDS (SDS-d25; pH 5.5). We selected SDS micelles to mimic an anionic, membrane-like environment and to stabilize the peptide for structural analysis as SDS provides high spectral resolution for backbone assignments and has been widely used in NMR studies to determine the structures of AMPs.14,92,93 We acquired homonuclear 2D-total correlation spectroscopy (TOCSY) with an 80 ms mixing time and nuclear Overhauser effect spectroscopy (NOESY) with a 300 ms mixing time, 5000 Hz spectral widths in both dimensions, and 512 increments in the indirect dimension. We also collected natural abundance 2D-13C-heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) and 13C-HSQC-TOCSY spectra with 128 scans to obtain 13C chemical shifts, which we used to derive the dihedral angles of the peptide using TALOS+.94 We processed and analyzed all NMR data using Topspin software version 3.2 (Bruker, MA, USA) and Sparky software version 3.115 (UCSF, CA, USA). A semi-automated assignment of NOESY cross-peaks was conducted using CYANA version 3.98.15,95 and all assigned peaks were manually verified for accuracy in Sparky. We performed the initial peptide structure calculation with 254 NOE-derived distance restraints and 22 dihedral angles. In the final calculation, we included 14 hydrogen bond restraints supported by NOESY patterns. We used 200 structures for the final calculation and selected the 20 lowest-energy structures to represent the WP-CAMPER1 structure ensemble.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation
We conducted MD simulations using membrane bilayers composed of DOPC (1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine) and DOPG (dioleoyl phosphatidylglycerol) at a 7:3 molar ratio, with each bilayer containing 64 lipids.12 We generated the initial WP-CAMPER1 structure using the AlphaFold2 Colab server96 and positioned the peptide parallel to the membrane surface, at least 1.5 nm above the upper leaflet. The simulations proceeded in two stages.97 First, we performed coarse-grained (CG) MD simulations using the MARTINI 2.2P force field for 500 ns to capture membrane-peptide association.98 We then selected representative CG frames corresponding to key events, specifically the initial membrane contact and the fully engaged state at 500 ns, and converted them into all-atom models. These all-atom systems were subsequently simulated for 10 ns using the CHARMM36 force field.98 All simulations were carried out using the GROMACS 2020.1-1 software package (Groningen, Netherlands), with system input files generated through the CHARMM-GUI server. We visualized the trajectories using Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD)99 and the trial version of BIOVIA Discovery Studio Visualizer (Accelrys Inc., SD, USA). We also simulated WP-CAMPER1 in membrane composed of POPG (1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1’-rac-glycerol) and CL (cardiolipin) (7:3 molar ratio), following the same protocol used for the DOPC:DOPG system, to evaluate its interactions with a bilayer enriched in PG and CL, the major anionic phospholipids of S. aureus membranes.100

Membrane depolarization
We measured bacterial membrane potential following an established protocol with minor modifications.90 We prepared an exponential phase culture of S. aureus MW2 in fresh TSB medium, washed the culture twice with PBS, and then resuspended it in twice the volume of PBS. To energize the bacterial cells, we added 25 mM glucose and incubated them for 15 minutes at 37°C. Next, we introduced 500 nM of DiBAC4(3) (bis-(1,3-dibutylbarbituric acid) trimethine oxonol) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, ON, Canada), a potential-sensitive probe that enters depolarized cells, binds to intracellular proteins or membranes, and exhibits enhanced fluorescence. We distributed 90 µL of the prepared bacterial culture into each well of a black, clear-bottomed 96-well plate (Cat. no. 3904, Corning, NY, USA) and monitored the fluorescence using a SpectraMax i3x (Molecular Devices, CA, USA) for 20 minutes, with excitation at 485 nm and emission at 520 nm, until a stable baseline was established. Afterward, we added 10 µL of serially diluted peptide solutions and recorded the fluorescence for an additional 40 minutes. We used Triton X-100 (1%) as a positive control.

SYTOX-based cell membrane permeability assay
We prepared exponential-phase S. aureus MW2 cells and diluted them in PBS to an OD600 of 0.2. We then added SYTOX Green (Molecular Probes, Life Technologies, Oregon, USA) to the cell suspension, achieving a final concentration of 5 μM, and incubated the mixture for 30 minutes at room temperature in the dark, following a previously established protocol.89 We distributed 90 µL of this dye/bacteria mixture into 10 μL of serially diluted 10× peptide solutions in black 96-well plates and measured the fluorescence for 1 hour at room temperature, using excitation and emission wavelengths of 485 nm and 525 nm, respectively.

Propidium iodide-based membrane permeability
We utilized a propidium iodide (PI) fluorescence-based bacterial permeation assay to investigate membrane-targeting interactions with the designed peptides, following a previously established protocol.89 We prepared exponential-phase S. aureus MW2 bacteria as described for the SYTOX assay, except that the final bacterial density was OD600 = 0.4 in PBS. We added PI dye to the bacterial suspension to achieve a final concentration of 2 µM. We measured fluorescence using excitation at 584 nm and emission at 620 nm for 1 hour at room temperature.

ATP release assay
To assess the ATP leakage potential of the peptides, we used a luciferase-based assay.101 We began by washing exponential-phase S. aureus MW2 bacteria three times with PBS (pH 7.4) and then adjusted the cell suspension to an OD600 of 0.4 in PBS. After treating the bacteria with 32 µg/mL of WP-CAMPER1 peptide at 37°C for 30 minutes, we centrifuged the cells at 14,000× g for 5 minutes. We transferred 50 µL of each supernatant to black, clear-bottomed 96-well plates containing 50 µL of BacTiter-Glo reagent (Promega, WI, USA) and measured the luminescence after 5 minutes of incubation at room temperature, as previously described.101

ΔpH measurement
We cultured S. aureus MW2 bacteria to mid-logarithmic phase, centrifuged the exponential-phase bacterial suspensions, and washed the cells three times with PBS (Gibco, MA, USA). We then resuspended the cells to an OD600 of 0.4 and incubated them with BCECF (1 µM) in the dark for 30 minutes at 37 °C. After staining, we treated the cells with peptides for 1 hour at 37 °C. We measured fluorescence intensity at 525 nm (excitation at 485 nm) using a Cytation 3 imaging reader (BioTek Instruments, VT, USA).

Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) detection assay
We quantified ROS levels in peptide-treated S. aureus MW2 using the fluorescent probe 2′,7′-dichlorofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA), a commonly used indicator of intracellular ROS.57 We cultured S. aureus MW2 to mid-logarithmic phase, washed the cells three times, and resuspended them in PBS (Gibco, MA, USA) to an OD600 of 0.4. We then stained the cells with DCFH-DA (100 μM) and co-incubated them with peptides at 10× MIC for 30 minutes at 37°C. We measured fluorescence intensity at 525 nm (excitation at 485 nm) using a Cytation 3 imaging reader (BioTek Instruments, VT, USA).

ROS-associated growth inhibition and spot titer assays
We evaluated the role of ROS in the antibacterial activity of peptides using spot titer and kinetic growth curve assays, following a previously established protocol57 with minor modifications. In a microplate growth curve assay, exponential-phase cultures of S. aureus MW2 were adjusted to 1×106 CFU/mL and incubated in 96-well plates (100 µL per well) with WP-CAMPER1 (1× MIC) in the presence or absence of NAC (10 mM). The optical density at 600 nm was recorded every 2 h to monitor bacterial growth kinetics using the SpectraMax 250 plate reader (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA). A decrease in bacterial killing efficiency in the presence of ROS scavengers indicated that ROS played a contributory role in the antibacterial mechanism of WP-CAMPER1.57

In a complimentary spot titer assay, exponential-phase S. aureus MW2 cultures were grown in TSB and diluted to approximately 1×106 CFU/mL. The bacterial suspensions were exposed to WP-CAMPER1 at 1× MIC in the presence or absence of the ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine (NAC, 10 mM). Cultures were incubated at 37 °C, and samples were collected at 0, 4, and 8 h, serially diluted, and plated on Remel™ TSA plates (Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) to determine surviving CFU after overnight incubation.

To assess the effect of higher bacterial and peptide concentrations, we also exposed 1×107 CFU/mL cultures to WP-CAMPER1 at 5× MIC, with or without NAC (10 mM). Samples were collected at 0, 4, and 18 h, and 20 µL from the culture was serially diluted, and plated on Remel™ TSA plates (Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) to quantify bacterial survival.

Lipid peroxidation assay
We assessed lipid peroxidation in S. aureus MW2 following peptide treatment using the fluorescent probe C11-BODIPY. We cultured the bacteria to mid-logarithmic phase, washed the cells three times, and resuspended them in PBS (Gibco, MA, USA) to an OD600 of 0.4. The cells were then stained with C11-BODIPY (2 μM) and co-incubated with peptides at 10× MIC for 30 minutes at 37°C. Fluorescence intensity was recorded at 525 nm (excitation at 485 nm) using a Cytation 3 imaging reader (BioTek Instruments, VT, USA).

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
We employed a modified established protocol to perform SEM imaging of S. aureus MW2 bacteria treated with the WP-CAMPER1 peptide.102 We treated 2 mL of an exponential-phase S. aureus MW2 culture (OD600 = 0.4, washed and resuspended in PBS) with 10× MIC of WP-CAMPER1 for 1 hour at 37°C. Following treatment, we centrifuged the bacterial cultures at 13,000× g for 10 minutes at room temperature. We fixed the bacteria with 50 µL of a fixing solution containing 2.5% glutaraldehyde in PBS buffer (pH 7.3) for over 1 hour at room temperature. After fixation, we placed a 20 µL droplet of the sample onto a (3-Aminopropyl) triethoxysilane (ANPTES)-functionalized silicon wafer and incubated it for 1 hour. We then thoroughly washed the silicon substrate in PBS (pH 7.3). To dehydrate the samples, we sequentially exposed the substrate to ethanol solutions of 20%, 40%, 60%, 90%, and 100% (v/v in water) for 5 minutes each. We then immersed the samples in tert-butyl alcohol (50% v/v in ethanol) for 5 minutes and allowed them to air dry. We mounted the samples on an aluminum SEM sample holder using double-sided carbon conductive tape. To improve the contrast of the SEM images, we coated the samples with a 5 nm thick Pt/Pd film using a magnetron 208HR High Resolution sputtering coater. We visualized the samples using a Nava Nano SEM 230 with a working distance of 5 mm, operating at room temperature and high vacuum (2E-6 Torr). During imaging, we set the electron beam diameter to 3 nm and the acceleration high voltage to 5 kV.

Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM)
We treated a 10 ml exponential-phase S. aureus MW2 culture (OD600 = 0.4, washed and resuspended in PBS) with WP-CAMPER1 at 20× MIC for 1 hour at 37 °C. For cryo-electron microscopy, bacterial samples were vitrified using a Leica EM-GP2® plunger (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany) on R2×2 Quantifoil® carbon holey film grids (Micro Tools GmbH, Jena, Germany), following established protocols.103 In brief, 4 µL of the treated suspension was applied to plasma-cleaned grids (Gatan Solarus 950), blotted with filter paper, and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane. Grids were stored in liquid nitrogen until imaging. For microscopy, grids were loaded into a JEM 2200FS electron microscope (JEOL Ltd, Akishima, Japan) operating at 200 keV, equipped with a field emission gun, an omega-type in-column energy filter, and a DE20 direct electron detector (Direct Electron Inc., CA, USA). Images were acquired using a 20 eV energy slit width, with a total electron dose of ~15 e⁻/Å² and a pixel size of 3.66 Å at the specimen level.

Use of S. aureus transposon mutants
We utilized S. aureus transposon mutants obtained from the Nebraska Transposon Mutant Library (NTML).104 This library includes 1,952 strains, each carrying a single mutation in a nonessential gene of the USA300 strain, a community-associated MRSA isolate.104 We specifically chose a mutant with a transposon insertion in the fmtc gene, which is responsible for transferring a lysyl group from L-lysyl-tRNA to membrane-bound phosphatidylglycerol (PG) to form lysylphosphatidylglycerol (LPG).59 LPG reduces the negative charge on the membrane, thereby enhancing bacterial virulence by providing a resistance mechanism against cationic AMPs.59

RNAseq assays
For RNA sequencing studies, we adhered to the protocol recommended by Novogene (Sacramento, CA, USA).105 We started with exponential cultures of S. aureus MW2 grown in TSB medium and adjusted to OD600 = 0.4. We treated 10 ml of this bacterial culture with 0.5× MIC of WP-CAMPER1 or water as a negative control for 30 minutes at 37°C with shaking at 180 rpm. Following treatment, we washed the bacteria three times with PBS and stored the pellet at -80°C. We extracted total RNA from the pellet and assessed its purity using a NanoPhotometer® spectrophotometer. RNA integrity and concentration were evaluated with the RNA Nano 6000 Assay Kit using a Bioanalyzer 2100 system. We also checked RNA degradation and contamination on 1% agarose gels. For transcriptome sequencing, we prepared libraries using 1 µg of RNA per sample with the NEBNext® UltraTM RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina® (NEB, MA, USA). We started by purifying mRNA from total RNA with poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads and then fragmented it using divalent cations in NEBNext First Strand Synthesis Reaction Buffer (5×). We synthesized cDNA using random hexamer primers and M-MuLV Reverse Transcriptase for the first strand, followed by DNA Polymerase I and RNase H for the second strand.106 Overhangs were converted to blunt ends with exonuclease/polymerase activities. We then adenylated the 3’ ends of the DNA fragments and ligated NEBNext Adaptors with hairpin loop structures for hybridization. To select cDNA fragments of the preferred length (150-200 bp), we purified the library fragments using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter, CA, USA). Next, to the size-selected, adaptor ligated cDNA, we added 3 µL USER Enzyme (NEB, MA, USA) at 37°C for 15 min followed by 5 min at 95°C before carrying out the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). We performed the PCR with Phusion High-Fidelity DNA polymerase, Universal PCR primers, and Index (X) Primer. We purified the PCR products with the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter, CA, USA) and assessed library quality using the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system (Agilent Technologies, CA, USA).

Fabrication and surface treatment of microfluidic devices for exponential phase MRSA persister killing
A silicon wafer master mold and a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)-based microfluidic device were manufactured as previously described.61 To inhibit biofilm formation during imaging, the lanes of the microfluidic device were pretreated with 0.1 M EDTA (Sigma Aldrich, MO, USA) for 10 min, Biofloat Flex coating solution (facellitate) for 30 min, and rinsed with MOPS buffer.61 For bacterial culture and cell loading, S. aureus USA 300 strain was grown overnight in tryptic soy broth (TSB) supplemented with 800 µg/mL Pluronic® F108 (Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA) at 37C and 220 rpm using an Excella E24 incubator shaker (New Brunswick scientific, NJ, USA). Cells were loaded into the microfluidic device using gel-loading tips (Fisherbrand™, NH, USA) by pipetting small volumes of culture directly into two lanes. To promote uniform cell loading into the device trenches, the chip was mounted onto a custom 3D-printed holder and centrifuged at 500 g for 5 minutes followed by 500 g for 15 seconds in the opposite direction, as previously described.61 After loading, and prior to imaging, excess inoculum was flushed out with fresh TSB containing 800 µg/mL Pluronic® F108.

For media delivery and antibiotic treatment, each lane was connected to a media reservoir flask with 0.02-inch internal diameter and 0.06-inch outer diameter Tygon tubbing (ND 100-80 Microbore Tubing, US plastic, OH, USA) and gauge 20, 1-inch, 90° stainless steel blunt Luer-lock needles (McMaster, GA, USA). A flow rate of 20 µL/min was maintained using an independent peristaltic pump in each lane (Longer Pump, Hebei Province, China).

The experiment followed a staged media exchange protocol. During the first 4 h, all device lanes were perfused with TSB containing 800 g/mL Pluronic® F108. Subsequently, the media was switched for 4 h to TSB with the same Pluronic® F108 concentration supplemented with 3.75 µg/mL of gentamicin which represented fifteen times the MIC for S. aureus USA 300 in a broth microdilution assay. Following exposure, the cells were incubated for an additional 16 h in fresh TSB with 800 g/mL Pluronic® F108 to assess gentamicin survival. Lanes with surviving trenches were further treated for 4 h with either TSB with 800 g/mL Pluronic® F108 and 60 g/mL WP-CAMPER1-d which also corresponds to fifteen times the bulk MIC or TSB with 800 g/mL Pluronic® F108 and 3.75 µg/mL gentamicin. This second treatment was followed by a final wash in TSB with 800 g/mL Pluronic® F108 to evaluate bacteria survival.

For microscopy, image acquisition and image analysis, phase contrast live-cell imaging was performed using the same microscope as described.61 Images were analyzed using a custom Python-based pipeline called TrenchCoat, as previously described.61 All image processing and data extraction were performed on the O2 High-Performance Computing (HPC) cluster at Harvard Medical School, MA, USA, which enabled parallel processing of large datasets. The resulting trench detection tables were used to generate kymographs using an additional custom-built Python script and FIJI macro.

For survival quantification and trench counts, the initial number of trenches was estimated by multiplying the number of FOVs imaged by 60 trenches per FOV. This method includes all trenches present in each FOV, regardless of whether a particular trench was empty at the beginning of imaging. Lineage survival was assessed visually after each first and second antibiotic treatment, based on the presence or absence of dividing cells in each trench. During non-antibiotic periods, we assumed that no cell death happened.

Serial passage assay
We evaluated the potential of WP-CAMPER1 and WP-CAMPER1-d to induce resistance in S. aureus MW2 using a serial passage assay adapted from a published protocol.107 On Day 1, we performed a standard MIC assay to establish baseline susceptibility. We defined bacterial growth as an OD600 ≥ 0.35. On each subsequent day, we initiated new cultures from the well that showed visible growth (OD600 ≥ 0.35) at the highest drug concentration. We diluted the selected culture 1:1000 in fresh TSB medium and performed a new MIC assay with a concentration gradient of the peptide or the control antibiotic. We repeated this procedure for 21 consecutive days. We included ciprofloxacin as a reference antibiotic. We recorded MIC values daily to track any changes in susceptibility over time.

Post-antibiotic effect (PAE)
We evaluated the post-antibiotic effect (PAE) of WP-CAMPER1, WP-CAMPER1-d, and ciprofloxacin against S. aureus MW2 following previously published methods108,109 with minor modifications. Briefly, overnight cultures of S. aureus MW2 were grown in TSB at 37 °C with shaking (220 rpm) and diluted in fresh TSB to obtain an inoculum of 2× 108 CFU/mL. We treated each 1 mL culture with WP-CAMPER1, WP-CAMPER1-d, or ciprofloxacin at 5× MIC for 1 h at 37 °C with shaking at 220 rpm. After treatment, we centrifuged the cultures at 16,000× g for 5 min to remove residual drug and washed the pellets three times with fresh TSB. The washed cultures were resuspended in drug-free TSB and incubated at 37°C with shaking (220 rpm) to allow regrowth. We collected samples immediately before and after drug removal and then at 1 h intervals. At each time point, we removed 10 µL of culture, performed serial dilutions in PBS, and plated them on TSA plates (BD Difco, NJ, USA). Plates were incubated overnight at 37 °C, and CFU were enumerated the following day. We calculated the PAE using the formula: PAE=T-C, where T was the time required for the treated culture to increase by 1 log10 CFU/mL from the count immediately after drug removal, and C was the corresponding time for the untreated control. Each assay, including its control, was performed in triplicate.

In vivo murine skin infection and treatment
We adapted a topical skin-abraded murine infection model with minor modifications to assess the in vivo efficacy of the WP-CAMPER1 designed peptides.110 Female C57BL/6 mice (6 weeks old; Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME, USA) were anesthetized via intraperitoneal injection of ketamine (90 mg/Kg) and xylazine (10 mg/Kg). The dorsal skin (~2 cm²) was shaved and tape-stripped seven times using Tensoplast® tape (replacing the tape each time) to disrupt the skin barrier and create a visibly damaged surface. To initiate infection, we applied 1 × 10⁷ CFU of S. aureus MW2 (exponential phase, suspended in PBS) in a 50 µL inoculum directly onto the damaged skin. For treatment, we applied 30 mg of peptide ointment (1% or 2% w/w in white petroleum jelly; Fisher Scientific, Cat. No. 19-090-843) at either 10 minutes post-inoculation (prophylactic model) or 24 hours post-inoculation (established infection model). Control groups received either petroleum jelly alone (negative control) or 2% commercial mupirocin ointment (positive control). Buprenorphine SR (0.5 mg/Kg) was administered for analgesia.

After 24 hours of treatment, mice were euthanized, and approximately 2 cm² of infected skin was excised. The skin tissue was homogenized in 1 mL PBS (Gibco), and 100 µL of the homogenate was serially diluted, plated on Remel™ TSA plates (Fisher), and incubated at 37°C for 18 hours to quantify viable bacteria. For cytokine analysis, 10 µL of EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail (Set III, Millipore Sigma) was added to 500 µL of the homogenate. Cytokine concentrations were quantified by Cytokine Core, LLC (Indianapolis, IN, USA) using a Luminex® MagPix™ platform following their in-house protocol.111

Deep-seated mouse thigh infection model
We evaluated the in vivo efficacy of WP-CAMPER1 designed peptides against S. aureus MW2 persisters using a modified neutropenic mouse thigh infection model.12 We rendered six-week-old female CD-1 mice (~25 g, Charles River Laboratories, Wilmington, MA, USA) neutropenic by administering cyclophosphamide intraperitoneally at 150 mg/kg on day -4 and 100 mg/kg on day -1 before infection. On the day of infection, we washed overnight cultures of S. aureus MW2 three times with sterile saline and diluted them to ~10⁷ CFU/mL. We injected 50 µL of the bacterial suspension into the right thigh muscle of each mouse. At 24 hours post-infection, we treated mice intraperitoneally every 12 hours for 3 days with either sterile water (vehicle control), WP-CAMPER1 or WP-CAMPER1-d (10 mg/Kg), or vancomycin (30 mg/Kg). We euthanized the animals at 96 hours post-infection. We collected blood via cardiac puncture to assess renal toxicity and excised the infected thighs aseptically. We weighed and homogenized the thigh tissue in PBS. For bacterial quantification, we serially diluted the samples, plated them on Remel™ TSA plates (Fisher Scientific, MA, USA), and incubated them at 37 °C for 18 hours. We expressed bacterial load as CFU per gram of thigh tissue. We analyzed blood urea nitrogen (BUN) (Life Technologies, MD, USA) levels using commercial kits according to the manufacturers’ protocols to evaluate liver and kidney function.

Statistical analysis
We used two-sided one-way ANOVA to compare multiple experimental groups or two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test to compare values between two groups. We considered a p-value of less than 0.05 as statistically significant for all experiments.

Data availability
The RNA-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession code PRJNA1282775 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/PRJNA1282775). The RNA-seq data are freely available without restriction. Values for all data points presented in the figures are provided in the Source Data file. The processed data generated in this study are included in the Source Data file and Supplementary Information associated with this article.

Code availability
The code generated in this study has been deposited in Zenodo and is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17781367.

### Reviewer 1

Shehadeh and Mishra et al. developed CAMPER, a hybrid AI pipeline combining a random forest classifier trained on ~3,600 AMP sequences with a mechanistic biophysical scoring functon(charge, hydrophobicity, helicity, amphipathicity) to prioritize α-helical, membrane-active peptides against antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The authors identified WP-CAMPER1, a mastoparans-derived 12-mer peptide with potent activity (MIC 4 µg/mL) against drug-resistant S. aureus strains. The team then carried out extensive characterizations and showed that WP-CAMPER1 kills exponential and stationary-phase persisters and disrupts biofilms. They also carried out RNA-seq analysis and revealed transcriptional changes across hundreds of genes with broad stress responses. D-enantiomer of this peptide (WP-CAMPER1-d) showed promising activity while providing a substratial advantage of proteolytic stability. The in vivo experiments with both WP-CAMPER1 and WP-CAMPER1-d in different contexts are unique strengths of the study. This combined method of ML-based S. aureus-specific model and the biophysical scoring is a promising approach toward the discovery of pathogen-specific AMPs, natural or synthetic. This work demonstrates how collecting pathogen-specific data and training an ML model could result in potent AMPs against a target pathogen. The manuscript is very well written, and the progression of experiments is logical and easy to follow. I have minor concerns that should be addressed before considering this work for publication: -In L152-154, the authors mention the improvement in CAMPER performance compared to RF model in false positives. This is misleading when the false negative has a dramatic increase (60 to 256 from RF to CAMPER). -In line with the previous comment, in Figure 2, comparisons of the models, CAMPER should also be added and the authors should provide a solid justification why, despite a decrease in AUC for CAMPER, this is still beneficial. -The work introduces mastoparan peptides (supplementary figure 9) as the design template but provides no direct comparisons of them with CAMPER peptides. Without testing mastoparans in the same conditions, how can one evaluate the degree of improvement achieved by CAMPER? For the in vitro assays (MIC, cytotoxicity and hemolysis) three diverse mastoparans from supplementary figure 9 should be tested.

### Reviewer 2

In this study, the authors propose a biophysics-based scoring function for antimicrobial peptides and integrate it with machine learning predictions to prioritize membrane-targeting peptides effective against persister and biofilm forms of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. While the authors have conducted extensive biological characterization, the manuscript needs some revision to be further considered for publication in Nature Communications. In particular, a more thorough literature review should be provided to better reflect recent advances in antimicrobial peptide prediction. 1. The novelty of this work primarily lies in incorporating biophysical properties of antimicrobial peptides (such as hydrophobicity, net charge, and α-helical propensity) into machine learning-based prediction. However, many existing studies have already considered these factors as part of their screening processes (Meher PK et al, Predicting antimicrobial peptides with improved accuracy by incorporating the compositional, physico-chemical and structural features into Chou’s general PseAAC. Porto WF et al, CS-AMPPred: an updated SVM model for antimicrobial activity prediction in cysteine-stabilized peptides. Bhadra P, AmPEP: Sequence-based prediction of antimicrobial peptides using distribution patterns of amino acid properties and random forest). The authors should thoroughly review these prior works in the Introduction and better clarify the unique contributions of their study. 2. Some of these previous studies have used such biophysical features directly as input to ML models. It is strongly recommended that the authors concatenate the features used in their scoring function into the input of an XGBoost/RF model as a baseline model, and compare performance on the test set. This would more convincingly highlight the value of the proposed scoring function. 3. Figure 1 could be improved to more clearly convey the overall workflow and enhance visual clarity. For example, the numerous arrows in the scoring function module may be confusing to readers, and the sources of the input sequences at the top should be labeled more specifically. 4. In the confusion matrix for XGBoost in Figure 2B, the total number of actual negatives is 224, which differs from Random Forest and Logistic Regression (both showing 314). The authors should carefully verify whether the data shown are correct. 5. In Figures 2G–J, the meaning of “n” and the percentages is unclear. Please clarify these elements in the figure legend. 6. Some regions in Figures 2G–J show a marked drop in precision. It would be beneficial to include a discussion of this observation in the main text to help interpret the potential causes. 7. It is confusing that different control groups were used for different experiments in Figure 3. 8. Figure 3 is too large, and the results for MRSA and VRSA are quite similar. It is recommended that the VRSA data be moved to the Supplementary Information for clarity. 9. In the screening process described above, all training data were L-form peptides. I wonder why D-form peptides were used in the animal experiments. Although D-forms improve stability, WP-CAMPER1-d did not appear to exhibit significantly better efficacy in Figure 5; on the contrary, it showed increased toxicity, as indicated by a significantly lower LD50.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript by Shehadeh et al. introduces CAMPER, a dual-component framework for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery against S. aureus that combines (i) a random-forest classifier trained on DBAASP-curated peptides and (ii) a mechanistic biophysical scoring function emphasizing charge, hydrophobicity, hydrophobic moment, and helicity. The DBAASP set is binarized (MIC ≤32 µg/mL = active; ≥64 µg/mL = inactive) and split 80/20 for model evaluation; the RF achieves ~80% accuracy (precision 81%, recall 86%, AUC 85%) and integrating the biophysical scorer raises precision to 86% and reduces false positives (84→27). CAMPER prioritized a mastoparan-derived peptide, WP-CAMPER1, and its D-enantiomer (WP-CAMPER1-d), which show membrane-targeting activity supported by NMR/MD and cell-based assays, broad transcriptional effects by RNA-seq, anti-biofilm/anti-persister activity including single-cell “Mother Machine” eradication of gentamicin-induced persisters, and efficacy in murine skin and deep-thigh infection models; toxicity was profiled in vitro (RBC hemolysis, HepG2/HaCaT/HKC LD50s) and by blood urea nitrogen analysis in vivo. Overall, this is a potentially promising study. However, the following comments need to be addressed prior to further consideration. Specific comments: 1. The activity labeling excludes MICs in 32–64 µg/mL, which can inflate apparent separability and precision. The authors should justify this binning and provide sensitivity analyses with alternative thresholds or ordinal/continuous modeling. 2. The authors should use a homology-aware split (e.g., cluster at ≥70–80% sequence identity and split clusters) to prevent near-duplicate sequences across train/test. They should report performance under such splits and with strict per-source or per-strain splits, and add an external holdout set. (Current split is random 80/20.) 3. Feature engineering choices need justification and ablation. For example, the authors compute 66 physicochemical descriptors plus 2048-bit Morgan fingerprints (features designed for small molecules rather than peptides). The authors should justify the peptide relevance of each class and include ablations comparing: (a) sequence embeddings (e.g., ESM/ProtBERT), (b) learned n-gram/CNN/RNN/Transformer baselines, and (c) the current RDKit/Biopython+Morgan approach. Those features driving gains should be reported. 4. ROC and PR curves with AUROC/AUPRC and 95% Cis should be shown; including calibration plots and class-balance details. Clarify threshold selection and report variance over multiple random seeds/splits. 5. When combining the RF with the biophysical scorer, the authors should detail how the two components are integrated (weighted sum? rank aggregation?). Include a formal ablation showing each property’s marginal utility and hyper-parameter sweeps for the sigmoid thresholds. 6. NMR structures were determined in 80 mM SDS micelles (pH 5.5); SDS can exaggerate helicity and is not a close mimic of the S. aureus membrane. The authors are encouraged to add spectra in milder, more physiologic mimetics (e.g., DPC micelles, lipid vesicles with PG/CL, etc.) and/or lipid titrations. 7. MD simulations use a DOPC:DOPG (7:3) bilayer. The authors should provide rationale and, ideally, additional runs with S. aureus–like compositions (higher PG/CL; lower PC) and longer all-atom trajectories (>2 ns AA) to support stable insertion conclusions. 8. The authors note uncertainty whether ROS arises secondarily from membrane damage. I feel like this should be explored further. For example, the authors could test ROS involvement (e.g., with ROS scavengers) and clarify causality. 9. The Mother Machine experiment reports ~4,320 trenches and eradication of three surviving lineages with WP-CAMPER1-d vs. gentamicin. I feel like this should perhaps be repeated across biological replicates, quantify CI on survival frequencies, and test additional antibiotics/conditions to generalize the effect. Authors should provide raw lineage-tracking data/videos as SI. 10. Minor: For biofilms, MBEC/MBIC determinations should be done against multiple clinical isolates and matrix characterization (eDNA/protein/polysaccharide). 11. In vivo experiments: The authors should report full dosing regimens, randomization/blinding procedures, group sizes per arm, and effect sizes with CIs for skin and thigh models. 12. It does not make sense to me that the positive control in the thigh infection model (i.e., vancomycin) did not reduce the bacterial load (e.g., Fig. 5H). 13. The authors could assess resistance potential (serial passage) and post-antibiotic effect. A “resistance-proof” implication should be avoided unless tested experimentally. 14. The authors should provide: (i) the exact train/validation splits, (ii) the labeled DBAASP sequence table with all preprocessing, (iii) scripts to reproduce figures/tables, and (iv) a model card with limitations. 15. The authors should clarify the definition of “Class A peptidomimetics,” and ensure sequences for WP-CAMPER1/analogs (and any non-standard residues) are disclosed in the main text or SI. The LM and D-forms’ therapeutic windows should be tabulated alongside MICs, hemolysis, and LD50s for direct comparison.
